html:
A trade treaty signed in 1838 between the Ottoman Empire and Britain, at Balta Liman on the Bosphorus. It opened the whole empire to British merchants on some of the most free trade terms of the age.

The Ottoman state agreed to end its trade monopolies, under which state agents bought up goods cheaply and sold them at a profit, and to tax foreign trade at low fixed rates. British merchants could buy and sell anywhere in the empire.

Sultan Mahmud II had a political reason. His rebel governor in Egypt, Muhammad Ali, was building factories and an army on the profits of state monopolies. If the treaty applied in Egypt too, it would cut his income, and Britain would back the sultan against him. Britain did so in 1840.

The treaty fits the reform era of the Tanzimat, which began the next year. Its longer effects are debated. Cheap British cloth flooded Ottoman markets and hurt local weavers, while exports of raw goods such as grain, cotton and silk grew. Similar treaties with other European states followed.
sum: A trade treaty signed in 1838 between the Ottoman Empire and Britain, at Balta Liman on the Bosphorus. It opened the whole empire to British merchants on some of the most free trade terms of the age.
